s: Good morning.
Can I see your identification, please?
Sure, here you are.
Thank you.
Now, in this first part, I'd like to ask you some questions about your life.
Let's talk about work or studies.
What subjects are you studying?
I studied electrical engineering.
It's a mix of physics, maths, circuits and power systems — technical, but practical too.
And that's the part I liked: you can see the theory in equipment people use every day.
Do you like your subject?
Hmm, I wouldn't call it my passion, but I do find it meaningful, and I'm happy enough to stay in the field.
What I enjoy is solving actual real-world problems — that never gets boring.
Why did you choose to study that subject?
Honestly, it wasn't my choice.
Back home people think an electrical engineering degree gets you straight into the power grid — stable, decent pay.
So my parents pushed me towards it.
It did suit my physics strength.
Do you think that your subject is popular in your country?
Yeah, quite popular actually.
Like I said, people assume an electrical engineering degree gets you into the power grid, and the pay there is decent — so a lot of students go for it.
Do you have any plans for your studies in the next five years?
Yeah, the plan is to go abroad and do a master's in engineering.
Then I'll use the courses and internships to work out which area suits me — I don't want to lock that in too early.
What are the benefits of being your age?
The big one is that you've still got room to experiment.
A wrong call now is far easier to fix than it'd be in ten years.
That's what gives me the confidence to switch direction.
Do you want to change your major?
No, not really.
Switching fields would cost me a huge amount of time, and honestly, I haven't come across anything that suits me obviously better.
So I'd rather stick with it.
Do you prefer to study in the mornings or in the afternoons?
Mornings, definitely.
It's cooler, and my head's just clearer.
In the afternoon I get so sleepy — I'll read the same page three times and take nothing in.
How much time do you spend on your studies each week?
Around thirty hours a week at the moment.
But I do block out time for exercise and for seeing friends as well, otherwise I'd burn out pretty quickly.
Are you looking forward to working?
Not massively, to be honest — my head's in further study right now.
I do miss having a salary come in every month, I'll admit that.
But going back to work is a later problem.
What technology do you use when you study?
Just a laptop, online courses, and this little IELTS practice website I built myself.
They're all useful — as long as I'm still the one doing the actual thinking, you know?
What changes would you like to see in your school?
I'd love to see more project-based learning, and closer links with industry.
I think theory sinks in so much better once you've actually seen what it's used for.
What work do you do?
I used to be an electrical engineer at Guangdong Power Grid.
My job was mainly testing and diagnostics — basically running equipment checks to work out whether the electrical assets were running normally or not.
Why did you choose to do that type of work (or that job)?
Well, it lined up with my degree, and it was stable — which mattered a lot to me straight out of university.
It was just the most direct path available at the time.
Do you like your job?
I respected it, definitely.
But I couldn't see myself doing it for the next thirty years.
That's actually one of the main reasons I left to prepare for postgraduate study.
What requirements did you need to meet to get your current job?
An electrical engineering degree, the technical knowledge obviously, and you had to stick to strict safety and testing standards.
They also cared whether you were careful by nature — a small mistake there can go badly wrong.
Do you have any plans for your work in the next five years?
The plan is to finish a master's, figure out which engineering direction fits me, and hopefully pick up some international work experience along the way.
I'm deliberately keeping the exact job open until I know more.
What do you think is the most important at the moment?
Right now it's just to keep learning without wrecking my health.
Both of those matter far more to me than rushing back into a job.
Do you want to change to another job?
I don't want to walk away from engineering completely.
But I might move into a different branch of it, once the master's and a few internships have given me a better picture.
Do you miss being a student?
Yeah, sometimes.
Mostly I miss having classmates around — people to grab food with, go to the gym with.
Student life was just naturally more social than living on your own.
What technology do you use at work?
Testing instruments, monitoring systems, diagnostic gear — that kind of thing.
Accuracy really mattered, because whatever number you got fed straight into decisions about the equipment.
Plus ordinary office software for the reports.
Who helps you the most?
And how?
Probably a senior colleague of mine.
She taught me how to read test results against the standards, and honestly, how to keep myself safe on site.
I owe her a lot.
Now, let's talk about your home or accommodation.
What kind of house or apartment do you want to live in in the future?
Down the line I'd love a detached house.
Quieter, better privacy, decent sound insulation — and if it came with a garden, even better.
Are the transport facilities to your home very good?
Yeah, pretty good.
There are buses and shared bikes right nearby, and public transport covers both short hops and longer trips.
I can get everywhere without owning a car, which suits me.
Do you prefer living in a house or an apartment?
For where I am right now, an apartment just makes more sense.
Long term though, I'd go for a house — I really do care about privacy and having things quiet.
Please describe the room you live in.
It's clean, pretty simply furnished — a bed, a desk, some storage, and a small balcony off it.
Nothing fancy, but it's comfortable for one person.
What part of your home do you like the most?
The balcony, easily.
Best view, loads of natural light, fresh air.
It's where I go when I need a quick break from studying, even if it's only ten minutes.
How long have you lived there?
Only about two months, so it's still quite new to me.
I'm slowly making it feel a bit more like mine — a few plants, my own stuff on the shelves.
Do you plan to live there for a long time?
No, not really.
It works for my study routine right now, but I'd like to move back home at some point and spend more time with my parents.
What’s the difference between where you are living now and where you have lived in the past?
The rented place gives me way more freedom and privacy.
Home is livelier — there's always someone around.
I like both, honestly, but living alone works better for how I'm studying at the moment.
Can you describe the place where you live?
It's a small rented apartment in Chenzhou.
Clean, quiet, and it's got all the basic furniture and appliances I need.
Nothing fancy, but it does the job for one person.
What room does your family spend most of the time in?
Honestly?
We mostly just stay in our own bedrooms scrolling on our phones, because the AC in the living room barely works.
We do catch up over meals though — that's when we actually talk.
What's your favorite room in your apartment or house?
At my current place it's the balcony, no question.
Back at my family home, it'd be the dining area — just because that's where everyone actually talks to each other.
What makes you feel pleasant in your home?
Cleanliness, appliances that actually work, comfortable furniture, and a quiet atmosphere.
That's basically it.
I don't need anything luxurious — I just want the place to function and feel settled.
Do you think it is important to live in a comfortable environment?
Yeah, definitely.
It affects your sleep and your concentration.
But comfortable doesn't have to mean big or expensive — for me, being quiet and having a reliable routine matter way more than fancy decoration.
Do you live in an apartment or a house?
An apartment — a rented one.
It's a practical size for one person, so it doesn't feel empty.
I'd like a house eventually, but not at this stage.
Who do you live with?
I live on my own at the moment.
Loads of privacy, and I get to run my day however I want.
The only downside is it can get a bit too quiet sometimes.
What do you usually do in your apartment?
During the week I get back pretty late, so honestly I mostly just sleep there.
Weekends are different — I'll read, or do some coding, cook something simple, get the housework done.
What kinds of accommodation do you live in?
A small rented apartment.
Not exactly spacious, but it's got all the basics.
There's a balcony too, which I really like — I've stuck a chair out there so I can sit and relax.
Let's talk about your hometown.
Where is your hometown?
Chenzhou, in Hunan Province.
It's a green, medium-sized city surrounded by mountains — a lot quieter than somewhere like Guangzhou or Shenzhen, which is partly why I like being back.
Is that a big city or a small place?
Medium-sized, I'd say — definitely not a huge metropolis.
Day-to-day life is pretty calm, although the tourist spots do get packed during the holidays.
Please describe your hometown a little.
It's green, it's mountainous, and it's pretty humid because it rains a lot.
Lovely natural scenery, and the pace is much slower than in China's biggest cities.
How long have you been living there?
I grew up there and stayed until I left for university.
And I'm back living there now.
So even though I spent a few years elsewhere, it's still the place I know best.
Do you think you will continue living there for a long time?
Not forever, necessarily.
I'll probably leave for postgraduate study or work.
But I'd still want to go back regularly and spend time with my parents.
Do you like your hometown?
Yeah, I do.
It's the greenery, the slower pace, and how familiar everything is.
The job market's limited, I'll admit — but it's a really comfortable place to live.
Do you like living there?
Yeah, especially right now.
It gives me a comfortable place to study and I get to stay close to my family, which matters while I'm preparing for all this.
What do you like (most) about your hometown?
The scenery and how relaxed it is, mainly.
You've got mountains and green space right on your doorstep — I can be on a proper trail within half an hour.
Is there anything you dislike about it?
The main thing is there just aren't that many jobs for young people.
You don't get many big private companies or specialised roles.
What's your hometown famous for?
Recently a newly developed scenic area blew up nationwide, so these days the city's getting known for tourism and its natural scenery.
Did you learn about the history of your hometown at school?
Yeah, we did.
We covered the Xiangnan Uprising — southern Hunan, 1928, and it involved areas around Chenzhou.
It stuck with me because I actually knew some of the places they mentioned.
Are there many young people in your hometown?
Yeah, but a lot of them head off to bigger cities — more jobs, more options.
The ones who stay usually do it for the lower cost of living, or to be near family.
Is your hometown a good place for young people to pursue their careers?
It's comfortable, but probably not ideal if you're really ambitious.
The stable jobs are pretty much all in public institutions and a handful of employers.
Have you learned anything about the history of your hometown?
Yeah, the basics.
I know about the Xiangnan Uprising and a few local traditions — but I definitely wouldn't call myself a history buff.
Did you learn about the culture of your hometown in your childhood?
Yeah, just the basics really — local traditions, a few big historical events.
It was never taught as its own proper subject, so most of what I know came from family.
Now I'd like to ask you about the city you live in.
What city do you live in?
Chenzhou, in Hunan — which is also my hometown.
I moved back fairly recently, after a few years studying and working in other cities.
Do you like this city?
Why?
Yeah, I do.
It's green, it's pretty relaxed, and you can get out into nature far more easily than you could in a big coastal city.
How long have you lived in this city?
I grew up there, left for university and then work, and came back recently to prep for IELTS.
So all in all I've spent most of my life there — just not in one continuous stretch.
Are there big changes in this city?
Yeah, definitely.
Tourism has taken off since that new scenic area went viral, and the city gets a lot busier during the holidays now.
Is this city your permanent residence?
It's my home base, I'd say.
But I might leave for postgraduate study and maybe work overseas, so I wouldn't call it permanent just yet.
Are there people of different ages living in this city?
Yeah, all sorts — kids, working adults, and quite a lot of older residents, especially in the older neighbourhoods like mine.
That mix makes the place feel balanced, rather than built for just one age group.
Are the people friendly in the city?
Generally, yeah.
Life moves slower, so people tend to actually know their neighbours — which isn't really the case in a massive city.
Is the city friendly to children and old people?
Fairly friendly, I'd say.
It's not overcrowded, there are parks, and the basic services are there.
But it's still not as easy to get around as it could be for everyone.
Do you often see your neighbors?
Yeah, pretty often.
I know a few of them because they're connected to my parents' workplace.
I bump into familiar faces near the entrance, or when I'm out for a walk around the block.
What's the weather like where you live?
Rainy and humid for most of the year, unfortunately.
Autumn's probably my favourite — it's cooler and relatively dry, so it feels much more comfortable.
Would you recommend your city to others?
Yeah, definitely — especially if you're into mountains, greenery, that slower kind of trip.
I'd just warn them that the traffic during the holidays can be brutal.
Finally, let's talk about the area you live in.
Do you like the area that you live in?
Yeah, I do.
It's quiet, the neighbours are friendly enough, and getting around is easy enough for daily life.
It's not exciting, I'll be honest — but it works for how I live right now.
Where do you like to go in that area?
There's a mountain nearby I like to hike up.
The vegetation's really dense, so it stays much cooler up there than down on the streets in summer.
Do you know any famous people in your area?
No, not that I know of.
It's mostly just ordinary families — including a few of my parents' colleagues and their relatives.
It's that kind of neighbourhood.
What are some changes in the area recently?
The biggest one is way more visitors, ever since a nearby scenic spot took off online.
The area feels livelier, but the traffic on holidays is definitely worse.
Do you know any of your neighbors?
Yeah, quite a few.
A lot of people there know each other because their families have lived or worked in the area for years.
We're not close friends, but we always say hello.
Are the people in your neighborhood nice and friendly?
Yeah, on the whole.
People say hello, and they'll help you out with small practical things — like taking in a delivery for you, or letting you know what's going on with the building.
Do you live in a noisy or a quiet area?
It's usually quiet, which is honestly one of the main reasons I like it.
You get the odd bit of traffic or renovation noise, but it's not a constant thing.
Thank you.
That's all for Part 1.
Now I'm going to give you a topic.
You will have one minute to prepare, and you should talk for one to two minutes.
You can make some notes if you wish.
Here is your topic.
Okay.
Describe a recent change in your plans.
You should say what the change was, why you made it, and how you feel about it now.
You have a moment to prepare.
When you're ready, please begin.
So the biggest change I've made recently was quitting my job at Guangdong Power Grid to prepare for a master's abroad.
I'd been there as an electrical engineer for about a year and a half.
It was stable, and when I first graduated I genuinely thought stability was what you should aim for.
But being in the job showed me I cared about other things too — growing, international experience, having more options later.
It wasn't an overnight decision, though.
I went through engineering programmes, worked out the costs and risks, and talked it over with my family.
The plan now is to get my English up, finish a master's in engineering, then use the courses and internships to figure out which area suits me.
I'm not running away from electrical engineering — I want to build on it.
It was uncomfortable, I won't lie — I gave up a steady salary and a routine I knew inside out.
But it made me feel much more responsible for my own future.
And it changed how I think.
I used to assume the safe path was always best.
I still value stability, but now I'd say long-term development deserves equal weight.
Thank you.
Let's move on to another topic.
Describe a program or app you created.
You should say what it was, why you made it, what problems you had, and how you feel about it.
You have a moment to prepare.
When you're ready, please begin.
So the program I want to talk about is one I built myself — a pretty simple IELTS practice website.
What I wanted was one place where I could organise speaking questions, record my answers and get AI feedback on them.
There were tools that did bits of it, but nothing matched the workflow I had in my head, so I built a small version.
The trickiest bit by far was getting the recording and the feedback to work together reliably.
Sometimes an audio file would upload fine but the page wouldn't recognise it.
Other times the AI response came back attached to completely the wrong question.
So I had to read the documentation, strip the process right back, and test every step on its own.
It took a fair bit of imagination too, because I had to picture how someone would move through the site before I knew how to build it.
It's still a personal prototype rather than a polished product, but I use it all the time.
What I like most is that it turned a vague idea into something real.
Thank you.
Let's move on to another topic.
Describe a person who helped you solve a problem.
You should say who the person was, what problem you had, how they helped, and how you felt.
You have a moment to prepare.
When you're ready, please begin.
So the person who really helped me out at work was a senior colleague at Guangdong Power Grid.
When I was new to high-voltage testing, I could operate the instruments fine — that wasn't the problem.
What I struggled with was reading a strange result and knowing what it actually meant.
And instead of just giving me a quick yes or no, she walked me through a proper method.
We'd compare the result against the technical standard and previous readings, check the temperature and humidity, double-check the connection — and only then decide whether it needed retesting.
I thought that was really clever, because it chipped away at the uncertainty step by step rather than relying on gut feeling.
And she was so patient with the younger ones — she'd explain the reasoning instead of just handing us the answer.
After that I used the same checklist on every test.
I'd still ask for help when I needed it, obviously — but I could explain my own reasoning first, instead of just shoving a number under her nose.
Thank you.
Let's move on to another topic.
Describe a person who overcame a difficulty.
You should say who the person is, what difficulty they faced, what they did, and why you admire them.
You have a moment to prepare.
When you're ready, please begin.
The person in my family I'm probably proudest of is my grandfather.
Back in the early sixties, he studied at a good university — but the main foreign language there was Russian, not English.
Then years later, once he was well into his career, he suddenly needed to pass an English exam to qualify as a senior engineer.
And the problem was, he had basically zero English, and he was still working full-time.
So he studied after work — started right from the beginning, basic vocabulary, basic grammar — and just kept going, even though the progress was painfully slow.
There were no apps back then, no online courses, nothing.
It was books and sheer consistency.
And eventually he passed, and got the qualification he'd been working towards.
But it's not really the exam result that I admire.
It's that he was willing to be a complete beginner again as a grown adult.
And honestly, that hits pretty close to home now that I'm sitting here preparing for IELTS.
Whenever I get impatient about how slowly I'm improving, I remind myself he did it under far worse conditions and still got there.
Thank you.
Let's move on to another topic.
Describe a city you visited and would recommend.
You should say when you went, what you did, what you liked, and why you would recommend it.
You have a moment to prepare.
When you're ready, please begin.
A city I really loved visiting — and I'd happily recommend it to anyone — is Nanjing.
I went over from Hefei while I was at university, since the two are close enough to do as a weekend thing.
I set off on the Friday afternoon and stayed a couple of days.
I went round the historical buildings and sites, wandered through the older parts of the city, and picked up a lot about modern Chinese history along the way.
What I liked most was that you could see different periods of history sitting side by side in the city itself.
I'd recommend it to anyone who wants a bit more from a trip than shopping and photos.
You can hit the important sites without needing a whole week, and there's a nice balance of history, normal city life, and green space.
I'd go back in a heartbeat, honestly — one weekend nowhere near covered it.
And it was doable on a student budget too, because the journey from Hefei was so short.
It felt like a realistic little city break, rather than some big holiday you have to plan months in advance.
Thank you.
Let's move on to another topic.
Describe a famous person you would like to meet who is connected with a film or TV programme you enjoy.
You should say who the person is, what you watched, what you would ask them, and why you admire their work.
You have a moment to prepare.
When you're ready, please begin.
The famous person I'd really love to meet is Rowan Atkinson — the guy who plays Mr Bean.
I first watched it as a kid and I still find it funny now, which says something.
The humour's all in the facial expressions and the physical comedy.
I actually rewatched Mr Bean's Holiday not long ago.
The plot's dead simple — he travels across France, causes one misunderstanding after another, and keeps accidentally getting tangled up in other people's problems.
I put it on at home when I just wanted something easy, and that's exactly why I enjoyed it: there was no complicated plot to work out.
If I did get to meet him — at an interview or a fan event, say — the thing I'd ask is how he builds comedy that lands across languages.
Because that's genuinely impressive: a show from one country making people laugh in loads of different cultures.
That's the main reason I admire his work.
I'm not expecting a private chat or anything unrealistic like that.
Honestly, just hearing him break down one single scene in person would be fascinating — because the finished thing looks so effortless, when the timing behind it must be incredibly precise.
Thank you.
That's all for Part 2.
Now, in Part 3, I'd like to discuss some more general questions related to the topics we've talked about.
What are the benefits of working abroad for a short time?
I think a short stint abroad is a really good way to test whether that lifestyle actually suits you.
You pick up different technical standards, you're using English in a real workplace, and you see how people run meetings and work as a team.
That's exactly why an international engineering internship appeals to me.
Obviously there are downsides — visas, the language barrier, feeling lonely.
But with a short placement those risks are much easier to handle.
Thank you.
Let's look at another aspect of the topic.
Is it always important to make detailed plans?
Detailed plans can definitely help, especially when a goal has a few stages to it — but I don't think they should be set in stone.
For me, a plan is mainly there to show me the next step and flag when I'm falling behind.
When I decided to quit my job and prepare for postgraduate study, I compared programmes, costs, all the risks.
But I still can't tell you exactly which specialisation I'll end up in.
So I'd rather have a clear direction and adjust as I go.
Thank you.
Let's look at another aspect of the topic.
How can teachers make a class less boring?
I think the key is getting students to actually do something with the information.
If a teacher just talks at you for forty minutes, even a genuinely interesting subject starts to feel distant.
Whereas questions, little experiments, real-world examples — they give you a reason to stay switched on.
My physics teacher in junior high used to give me a hint rather than the full answer, so I had to finish the thinking myself.
And look, not every minute has to be entertaining.
But students should feel involved, rather than just copying down notes.
Thank you.
That concludes Part 3.
Good morning.
Can I see your identification, please?
Sure, here you are.
Thank you.
Now, in this first part, I'd like to ask you some questions about your life.
Let's talk about hobbies.
Do you have any hobbies?
Yeah.
My main one is hiking — I usually head up a mountain near my place at weekends, mostly to get away from screens and city noise for a bit.
Did you have any hobbies when you were a child?
As a kid I was really into outdoor group games — hide-and-seek with the other kids in my neighbourhood, mostly.
The good thing was you didn't need any equipment, so you could just start playing whenever.
Do you have a hobby that you’ve had since childhood?
Not exactly.
I've always liked being outdoors, but hiking only became a proper regular hobby once I was older and could travel around on my own.
Do you have the same hobbies as your family members?
Yeah, definitely.
My parents have had a big influence on me, especially with travelling and hiking.
They took me on trips all the time when I was younger, so I just grew into it.
Now, let's talk about your spare time.
Do you often have free time?
Yeah, although I build most of it around studying.
I do about thirty hours a week of learning, which still leaves me enough for exercise and seeing people.
What do you usually do in your spare time?
I'm an outdoors person, so I'll usually go hiking at the weekend.
Although if it's absolutely boiling out, I'd honestly rather stay in and watch funny videos.
Which day do you have more free time on, Saturday or Sunday?
Sunday, usually.
Saturday often has stuff left over from Friday hanging around, whereas Sunday feels properly separate from the week.
So that's when I can actually switch off and enjoy the day.
Would you like to have more free time in the future?
A bit more would be nice, sure.
But I don't need endless free time — I just want enough to rest without feeling like I've wasted the whole day.
Let's talk about walking.
Do you walk a lot?
Yeah, definitely.
I've always been into outdoor stuff, hiking especially.
And in daily life I'll usually walk rather than take a bike, as long as it's not too far.
Did you often go outside to have a walk when you were a child?
Yeah, all the time.
I was always out playing with the other kids from my neighbourhood — hide-and-seek was the big one — so walking and running around was just a normal part of the day.
Why do people like to walk in parks?
Well, parks are safer, greener and quieter than a busy street.
You can exercise without worrying about traffic.
And a park gives you a clear route, so the walk feels more relaxing and less aimless.
Where would you like to take a long walk if you had the chance?
I'd probably pick a mountain trail — somewhere with an open view and cooler weather.
A long walk feels way more rewarding when the scenery's actually changing around you.
Where did you go for a walk lately?
I went up the mountain near my place recently.
The vegetation up there is so dense that it stays surprisingly cool, even in the middle of summer.
Now I'd like to ask you about scenery.
Do you look out the window at the scenery when travelling by bus or car?
Not really, no — I get sleepy in a car, so I usually just nap through the journey.
I'd rather enjoy the scenery once I've actually arrived.
Do you prefer the mountains or the sea?
Mountains, definitely.
There are usually plenty of trees for shade, so I don't worry so much about getting burnt.
And I love hiking — it gives me that feeling of being close to nature.
Do you like to take scenery pictures?
Yeah, definitely.
I'm really into hiking, and I always take a camera with me.
What I enjoy is catching those moments where the light and weather make somewhere ordinary look special.
What are the most beautiful sights you have seen while traveling?
Probably a sunrise I saw on a two-day hike, up in a high-altitude part of Sichuan.
We had to get up ridiculously early for it, which honestly made it even more memorable.
Let's talk about views.
Do you like taking pictures of different views?
Yeah, definitely.
I love hiking and travelling, so all these different kinds of scenery really appeal to me.
I'll try to catch the moments where the light makes an ordinary place look special.
Do you prefer views in urban areas or rural areas?
Rural, I'd say, because being surrounded by nature just relaxes me.
That said, cities can look incredible at night — when all the lights come on, it looks almost cyberpunk.
Do you prefer views in your own country or in other countries?
Well, I've never actually been abroad, so I can't really compare.
But I'd love to travel once I've got the time and money, because I'm curious how the landscapes differ from China's.
Have you seen an unforgettable and beautiful view or scenery?
Yeah, definitely.
The one that stands out is a sunrise I watched on a hike with my girlfriend.
We started climbing at four in the morning, and the sky slowly changing colour made it worth it.
Now, let's talk about mornings.
Do you like getting up early in the morning?
Yeah, especially when I've got something important to study.
It's cooler, and my head is just much clearer than it is in the afternoon.
What do you usually do in the morning?
On weekdays I get up, wash, have breakfast and get straight into studying.
I try not to get sucked into my phone before I start, although that doesn't always work.
What did you do in the morning when you were little?
Why?
When I was little, I'd always try to talk my grandfather into taking me to the park near my kindergarten first.
Purely so I could put off going in — I was not a fan.
Are there any differences between what you do in the morning now and what you did in the past?
Yeah, quite a big difference.
My mornings as a kid were completely built around school and getting there on time, whereas now they're much more flexible and I set my own pace.
Do you spend your mornings doing the same things on both weekends and weekdays?
Why?
No, not really.
At the weekend I'll get up later, take my time over breakfast, and usually get some housework done before I decide what else to do.
Finally, let's talk about different stages of life.
What did you often do with your friends in your childhood?
We played a lot of hide-and-seek and other outdoor games — all the kids from the same neighbourhood.
We'd meet up after school and just keep going until our parents shouted at us to come home.
What do you think is the most important at the moment?
Carrying on with my studies while staying healthy — that's the main thing right now.
I really don't want exam prep to swallow up everything else.
Do you have any plans for the next five years?
I'm hoping to do an engineering master's abroad, get some practical experience, and work out which specialisation actually suits me best.
